name: strategy
intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one behind a common operation, and make them interchangeable, so the algorithm a context executes can vary independently of the context and its clients - including at run time.
problem: One class supports several variants of the same computation - sort orders, pricing or tax rules, routing and backoff policies, compression codecs - and the variant has to be selected at run time. Hard-wiring the variants into the class (or into one subclass per variant) mixes algorithm detail with the class's own logic, forces recompilation for every new variant, and turns selection into a growing conditional that runs on every call.
context: Applies when one context object owns the data but delegates one algorithm (or a small set of related algorithms) to a pluggable implementation, when the implementations share a stable operation signature, and when the choice is made at run time - from user input, configuration, request data or deployment - or from a closed family of variants that already differ in space/time or accuracy trade-offs. Typical homes: pricing, discount and tax calculation; sorting and comparison orders; routing, load-balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting policies; compression, serialization and encoding codecs; validation and normalization rules; numerical solvers chosen per problem.
benefits: Families of related algorithms become named, individually testable units instead of branches buried inside the context.
The algorithm varies independently of the context: a new strategy is added without touching the context or its clients (Open/Closed), and one strategy is reused by several contexts.
The conditional that selected behaviour disappears from the hot path: the choice is made once, at configuration or wiring time, instead of in a switch or if-chain on every invocation.
Replaces subclassing as the mechanism for behaviour variation: no subclass per variant, so the type count does not multiply and the behaviour can be changed while the object lives.
Algorithm-specific state and dependencies (credentials, tuning parameters, caches, negotiated formats) stay inside the strategy, out of the context and out of unrelated variants.
Creates a clean seam for dependency injection, configuration-driven wiring and testing: a fake or recording strategy exercises the context without the real algorithm.
tradeoffs: The choice does not disappear, it moves: somebody must know the alternatives and select one, so the conditional reappears in a factory, a configuration key or the caller - clients become aware of the algorithms even though the context is not.

One extra indirection per delegated call (virtual dispatch, function-pointer hop, std::function thunk or vtable lookup) plus an object where a method used to be; for a trivial algorithm on a cold path the type, the wiring and the indirection cost more than the branch they replaced.

More objects and types to own: a strategy per variant, plus whoever creates, configures and shares them; stateless strategies should be shared, which raises their lifetime and thread-safety questions.

The interface must be wide enough for every variant, so some strategies receive parameters they ignore, or the context passes itself and the strategies start reaching into it - the opposite of the decoupling that was the goal.

A strategy whose signature or semantics are subtly inconsistent (a non-total comparator, a codec that is not the inverse of its counterpart) fails at integration time, not at the type level; the contract is behavioural, not structural.

A stateful strategy makes the context's behaviour depend on state it does not own, and swapping a strategy at run time can leave context-side state (caches, negotiated parameters) derived from the old algorithm.
The context/strategy split hides a call chain: debugging, profiling and reading the code now jump through a delegate, and stack traces name the strategy, not the caller's intent.

Rule of Three applies: the pattern pays off when you genuinely have or expect at least three variants or a real runtime-swapping need - a single expected variant makes the interface and factory pure overhead.

Strategies that carry mutable internal state are hazardous in concurrent or shared contexts; each concurrent context that needs a strategy should receive its own instance, or strategies should be truly immutable.

participants.responsibility: Owns the invariant data the algorithm works on, holds a reference to one strategy object, and forwards the algorithm's invocation to it; it exposes how the strategy is supplied (constructor, setter, configuration) but never knows a concrete strategy type.
Declares the operation (or the small set of related operations) common to all supported algorithms, which the context calls through.

Implements one algorithm against the Strategy operation, usually stateless across invocations or owning its own configuration explicitly; it must not depend on the context's internal state beyond the data it is handed.

Creates the appropriate ConcreteStrategy - directly, through a factory, a registry or the dependency-injection wiring - configures the Context with it, and is the only place that knows the concrete type; in the function-value form it simply passes the function.

use_cases: Pricing, discount and tax calculation where the rule set is selected per customer, region or campaign and changes independently of the checkout or invoicing flow.

Sorting and comparison orders chosen by context - a UI column, a request parameter, a locale - which is how the JDK uses the pattern for Comparator in Collections.sort/List.sort and how C uses it for qsort's comparison function.
Routing and policy selection: path finding, load balancing, retry/backoff and rate-limiting algorithms chosen from configuration without editing the caller.
Compression, serialization and encoding codecs (gzip/deflate/zstd, JSON/Protobuf, character encodings) selected per stream, per record or per request.
Validation and normalization rule sets for pluggable document or form types, where each variant knows its own schema quirks and error format.
Numerical and scientific kernels: integration, interpolation or solver algorithms chosen per problem with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.
Pluggable authentication/authorization or hashing policies chosen per tenant, where the same code path must run different algorithms behind one signature.
E-commerce shipping provider selection (UPS, FedEx, DHL) where each carrier implements a different rate-calculation algorithm, and the shipping calculator is decoupled from the carrier specifics.
Payment processing gateways (credit card, virtual account, wallet) where each method has distinct validation, fee calculation and settlement rules, but the checkout flow is uniform.
Data retrieval at runtime: selecting between an API client, a web scraper, a database query or a cache-first lookup depending on availability, cost or latency requirements.
ML inference: choosing between ONNX, TensorRT, CPU or GPU backends for model execution, each with different latency/throughput trade-offs, selected per request or per deployment environment.
Travel and navigation: routing algorithms (walking, cycling, driving, public transit) with distinct distance/time/transfer calculations, chosen by user preference or real-time conditions.
Hybrid AI systems: combining symbolic decision logic with sub-symbolic ML model inference behind a uniform interface, enabling runtime selection of the reasoning strategy.
Log routing: dispatching log events to different backends (file, console, cloud observability platforms) selected by deployment environment or tenant configuration.
Encryption and cipher suites: selecting TLS cipher suites, password hashing algorithms (bcrypt, argon2), or encoding schemes based on security policy and compliance requirements.
File format processing: parsing and rendering strategies for documents, images, or data files where each format requires different handling but the pipeline remains uniform.
Game AI: selecting enemy behavior algorithms (aggressive, defensive, evasive, patrol) per entity type or difficulty level, enabling runtime personality changes.

Apache Kafka producers select or replace the partition-selection algorithm through the org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner interface (default sticky/key-hash, RoundRobinPartitioner for even distribution), configured per producer via partitioner.class.

Envoy proxy chooses one load balancing algorithm per upstream cluster from the envoy.load_balancing_policies extension category (ROUND_ROBIN, LEAST_REQUEST and third-party policies), each implementing one host-selection operation behind the cluster's router call path.

scikit-learn estimators expose interchangeable optimization algorithms behind one fit/predict API via the solver parameter (LogisticRegression: lbfgs, liblinear, saga, newton-cg, newton-cholesky), documented as a choice driven by dataset size and penalty rather than by a different client interface.
avoid_when: Only one algorithm exists and no second one is planned: a plain method (or a plain function) is simpler than an interface, a factory and a setter.

The variation is the object's own state machine, not a pluggable algorithm: that is the State pattern, where transitions between states are the point and behaviour follows the object, not the caller's choice.
The whole object's behaviour varies rather than one algorithmic step: Template Method (fixed skeleton with overridden steps) or plain polymorphism is the right shape.
The variants are a closed enumeration of trivial differences: a switch on an enum or a dispatch table expresses the same thing with less machinery and no extra types.

The choice must be made at build time for performance and the language offers zero-cost static dispatch: use template policies, generics or compile-time dispatch instead of a run-time strategy object.
The strategy would need the context's internals to do its job: relocating the algorithm and passing the context back in only moves the coupling into a new file.

The variants differ mainly in the data they carry rather than in their behaviour: a tagged union (discriminated union, sealed hierarchy, enum plus payload) models that more directly than a strategy per variant.
anti_patterns: "Strategy theater": an interface with exactly one implementation, kept for a hypothetical second algorithm - a type, a factory and a setter bought for nothing.
"Smart context": the context tests or casts the strategy (if isinstance(s, GzipStrategy)) to special-case behaviour, so strategies are no longer interchangeable.
"Selection inside the context": the conditional moved into the context's constructor or method that builds the strategy; the branch survived, the flexibility did not.
"One monster interface": the strategy interface grows a method per variant, so every strategy implements operations it does not need and the contract stops describing the family.
"Global-state strategy": strategies that read singletons or global configuration instead of receiving their parameters, so the swap is invisible and tests become order-dependent.
"Stale strategy at run time": the strategy is replaced while the context still holds state derived from the old algorithm (caches, negotiated parameters), producing mixed-up behaviour.
"Subclass per variant": one class hierarchy per algorithm combination instead of one strategy interface - the structure Strategy exists to replace.
"Resource leak through swap": a strategy holding open files, connections or native handles is swapped without clean release, leaking resources across the lifetime of the context.

"Serialization surprise": strategies that capture closures over mutable external state, or that reference types not available in all deployment environments, fail to serialize or deserialize correctly.
"Strategy explosion": breaking a simple algorithm into dozens of micro-strategies increases maintenance burden and obscures the design; consolidate when strategies differ only in trivial constants.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the context names only the strategy operation.
Encapsulate what varies: the algorithm family is isolated behind one operation while the context keeps the invariants.
Composition over inheritance: behaviour is delegated to a composed object instead of being hard-wired into a subclass.
Open/Closed principle: new algorithms are added without modifying the context or existing strategies.
Dependency inversion: the context depends on the abstraction, and the concrete algorithm is supplied from outside.
Single responsibility: selection belongs to the client or the wiring, execution belongs to the strategy, and the data belongs to the context.
Interface segregation: keep the strategy interface narrow; prefer multiple small operations over one bloated interface that forces strategies to implement unused methods.
best_practices: Design the strategy operation from what the algorithms genuinely share and keep it small; when variants need different inputs, pass an explicit request/data object instead of widening the interface or handing over the whole context.
Keep strategies stateless across invocations, or give each context its own instance; share only immutable configuration-only strategies and document the sharing and its thread-safety.
Put selection in exactly one place - the caller, a factory/registry or the dependency-injection wiring - and make the default explicit so no execution path runs without a strategy.

Prefer the lightest form the language offers: a function or lambda when there is a single operation, an object or interface when the strategy has configuration, several operations, or needs identity for logging, testing and configuration.
Name strategies after the algorithm they implement, keep each in its own unit, and test the context against a fake strategy that records the calls it receives.

Decide and document whether the strategy may change during the context's lifetime; if it may not, hold an immutable injected reference, and if it may, define what happens to state derived from the previous strategy.

Apply the Rule of Three: introduce an explicit strategy interface only when you have at least three concrete variants or a demonstrated need for runtime swapping; two variants usually justify a simple boolean or branch.
Use a Null Object strategy instead of null to represent 'no algorithm'; this keeps the interface uniform and avoids scattered null checks throughout the context.

When strategies hold resources (connections, file handles, native pointers), make disposal explicit - implement a close/Dispose/drop method and call it when the context is torn down or the strategy is replaced.
Document the thread-safety contract: strategies used across concurrent contexts must be stateless or immutable; if a strategy must be stateful, each concurrent context needs its own instance.

Consider serialization requirements early: if strategies are stored in session state, sent across service boundaries or cached, ensure all concrete types are available at deserialization and that captured closures or external references do not break.
Use Protocol or structural typing where available instead of explicit inheritance to reduce coupling between strategies and allow existing types to satisfy the contract without modification.
When using a registry or factory for strategy selection, validate inputs at the selection boundary and fail fast with a clear error rather than allowing an unknown strategy key to propagate.
Consider adding a describe or metadata method to strategies when debugging, logging or introspection is needed; this avoids runtime type inspection in the context.

related_patterns_notes.state: Both delegate behavior to a separate object via a common interface. State differs by modeling behavior that changes as the object's internal state transitions - states typically know about and initiate transitions to other states. Use State when the object's behavior changes based on its current state throughout its lifecycle; use Strategy when the algorithm is chosen once at configuration/wiring time and remains fixed during execution.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Both factor out algorithmic variation. Template Method uses inheritance to override specific steps of a fixed algorithm skeleton in a base class, varying parts at compile time. Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms at runtime. Use Template Method when the algorithm structure is stable and only specific steps vary; use Strategy when the entire algorithm is interchangeable and may change at runtime.
related_patterns_notes.command: Both encapsulate an operation behind an interface. Command typically carries both the action and its data (receiver, parameters), and commands are often queued, logged, or undone. Strategy encapsulates only the algorithm, focuses on selecting among interchangeable algorithms, and does not inherently carry execution context. Use Command for action-oriented tasks (undo/redo, queuing, logging); use Strategy for algorithm selection.
related_patterns_notes.bridge: Both use composition to decouple an abstraction from its implementation. Bridge separates two orthogonal hierarchies (abstraction and implementation) that can evolve independently. Strategy focuses on allowing the algorithm to vary at runtime. The patterns share the composition-over-inheritance principle but serve different decomposition purposes.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Both wrap other objects. Decorator adds behavior to an object without changing its class, typically stacking multiple decorators. Strategy replaces the algorithm wholesale. They compose well: a decorator can wrap a strategy to add concerns like logging, caching, or retry around a strategy's core algorithm.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Both delegate to a handler object. Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain until a handler processes it. Strategy selects exactly one algorithm from a family. Use Chain when multiple handlers may handle a request and the suitable handler is determined by the chain; use Strategy when exactly one algorithm must be selected and executed.
related_patterns_notes.policy-based-design: Policy-based design (C++) is the compile-time counterpart to Strategy. Using template policies, it selects algorithms at compile time with zero runtime overhead. Strategy uses runtime dispatch. Use policy-based design when the choice is known at build time and performance is critical; use Strategy when the choice must be deferred to runtime.
related_patterns_notes.dispatch-table: A simple functional alternative to Strategy for closed, fixed sets of variants. A dictionary or switch maps keys to functions. Use dispatch tables for trivial, stateless variants; use Strategy when variants grow in complexity, need configuration, or require runtime extensibility.
